masthead_title: Chips and power-sector stocks bounced hard Friday, but credit spreads widened again instead of easing — and a much hotter-than-expected jobs report pushed December rate-hike odds higher, not lower.
regime_line: The S&P 500 added a modest 0.31% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.09% Friday, clawing back a sliver of Thursday's rout as chip and AI-hardware names led — but HY and IG credit spreads widened again rather than confirming the bounce, the 2-year yield rose more than the 10-year on a jobs report that beat every forecast (165K vs. roughly 63K expected), and the 30-year Treasury's 5.26% keeps company with a level the bond market last routinely held before 2002, only briefly revisited in 2007 (History, below) — equities say relief, credit and the front end of the curve say otherwise.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — six open, none due yet

Every open conditional claim (§4B) is checked against Friday's close before any new narrative is written. None reached its deadline this run, but two are worth a close look — one because its missing half just arrived.

  • CL-0062 (jobs report vs. credit, due 2026-11-10, tomorrow): the print half of this claim is now in and it's unambiguous — October nonfarm payrolls rose 165K against a roughly 63K consensus (BLS release via Reuters/CNBC), unemployment fell to 4.1%, average hourly earnings rose 0.4% — a clean beat, nowhere near the 40K confirm-a-growth-scare line, comfortably past the 90K refute line on its own. But the claim's refute path needs both a strong print and HY/IG OAS easing back below |z| 1.5, and credit did the opposite: HY OAS z +2.83 (was +2.18), IG OAS z +2.78 (was +2.44), wider, not easing. That combination — strong print, credit still wide — is the exact mixed/inconclusive outcome the claim itself called out in advance. Friday's own OAS reading (the market's same-day reaction to the print) hasn't published yet — it lands on tomorrow's run, which also happens to be the deadline, so this closes out cleanly tomorrow rather than today.
  • CL-0063 (SMH durable repricing, due 2026-11-13): one of five sessions in — SMH closed $463.96 Friday, a 3.63% bounce off Thursday's $447.73 base, nowhere near either the $420 confirm line or the $480 refute line. Still open, still live either way.
  • CL-0058 (Oracle, due 2026-11-10, tomorrow): three of five sessions in — Oracle closed $116.10 Friday, below its $119.22 base but the “every session at or below base” confirm path broke on day one ($123.73) and stays broken; nowhere near the $130 refute line. One session left before the deadline.
  • CL-0059 (Gartner, due 2026-11-11): three of five sessions in — Gartner closed $190.10 Friday, its lowest close of the window, well below the $204.22 base; confirm path broke on day one, not a refute (needs $220).
  • CL-0060 (Vistra, due 2026-11-12): two of five sessions in, and the confirm path just broke — Vistra closed $124.80 Friday, above its $120.29 base (a bounce following Tuesday's Texas-election selloff and Thursday's bottom), breaking the “stays flat-to-lower” confirm condition; not a refute (needs $135). NRG, named in the claim but not part of its formal test, also bounced hard, $80.55 → $88.29.
  • CL-0061 (FIS, due 2026-11-12): two of five sessions in, confirm path intact — FIS closed $28.73 Friday, still at or below its $29.76 base both sessions so far; not a refute (needs $34).
story_html:
Friday's own coverage (The Washington Post, Fox Business, TheStreet) was straightforward: the Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42 and the S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86, a partial bounce from Thursday's rout, led by chip and AI-hardware names — Nvidia +2.8%, AMD +11%, SanDisk +nearly 4%. The Dow lagged, down about 0.46%. For the week, every major index still finished lower (Nasdaq −3.4%, S&P −2.7%, Dow −0.9%). The same morning brought the October jobs report: nonfarm payrolls +165K against a roughly 63K consensus, unemployment down to 4.1%, wages up 0.4% — a clean beat covered by Reuters, CNBC, and the BLS release itself. Multiple named outlets (Kitco, Morningstar, the South China Morning Post) tie that beat directly to a jump in December Fed rate-hike odds, to roughly 78–80% on CME FedWatch and prediction markets, up from about 67% before the print — the opposite of what a hot labor report would mean for cut odds, and consistent with the Oct. 27–28 FOMC's own 10–2 hold, where two dissents favored a hike outright.

This system's own pull backs those numbers and adds the piece the headlines treat as separate stories. The jobs beat and the rate-complex reaction aren't two stories; they're one. The 2-year yield rose 5bp to 4.51% Friday — more than the 10-year's 2bp (to 4.86%) or the 30-year's 1bp (to 5.26%) — a front-end-led move that flattened 2s10s by 3bp to 35bp, exactly the pattern Unit 1 (taught in August) says to expect when hot data represses the Fed's expected path rather than just nudging the term premium: the front end, not the long end, does the repricing. The dollar firmed 0.74% to 102.30 (newly flagged, z +1.64) in the same hawkish-repricing direction. But credit didn't confirm the equity bounce. HY OAS and IG OAS — both already flagged Thursday — widened again on Thursday's own print (dated with the usual one-day lag): HY OAS z +2.83 (was +2.18), IG OAS z +2.78 (was +2.44). Per this brief's own epistemics rule (§4C) and Unit 8's hierarchy (taught this week): when equities and credit disagree, credit gets the benefit of the doubt. Friday's bounce is real; it just isn't yet confirmed.

Two of the day's three qualifying movers were earnings- or analyst-driven, not drift: Axon fell 18.18% on an outright Q3 miss and cut guidance, while Coherent rallied 13.58% on a same-day Citi price-target raise following Thursday's post-earnings drop — a reminder that Thursday's “beat can still be a sell” lesson (Unit 6) can also run in reverse two sessions later once analysts re-price the same numbers (Movers, below).
dashboard_interp_html:
The front end of the curve did almost all of Friday's work, and it moved in the direction a hot jobs report points toward. The 2-year yield — the part of the curve that tracks Fed expectations most closely — rose 5bp to 4.51% (z +0.52; 49th percentile since 1977 but the 77th of the last 30 years, † — cite both). The 3-month bill rose 2bp to 4.19% (z +1.26, not flagged; 52nd/70th percentile, no real gap). The 10-year rose 2bp to 4.86% (z +0.39; 45th/81st, †) and the 30-year rose just 1bp to 5.26% (z +0.25; 46th/80th, † — today's lead History-check fact, below). Why this matters: when short rates move more than long ones on a single data point, the bond market is repricing how many more times the Fed moves, not how much growth or inflation risk gets priced in for the next decade — the kind of move that can nudge a new CD or a short-term savings rate before it touches a 30-year mortgage quote.

The curve itself flattened a touch on that front-end move: 2s10s narrowed 3bp to 35bp, 3m10y held flat at 67bp — both still comfortably positive, far from the inversion that shows up on this morning's longer-run watch-list (History, below).

Credit, by contrast, widened again — the day's real divergence. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, dated Thursday 11-05, the usual one-day lag) rose 16bp to 3.48% (z +2.83, flagged, now this run's largest Tier 1 flag; 87th percentile of its own ~3-year record, §4F, marked *). IG OAS, the investment-grade equivalent (also dated 11-05), rose 2bp to 0.93% (z +2.78, flagged; 74th percentile of its own ~3-year record, also *). SOFR, the overnight bank-to-bank borrowing rate (also dated 11-05), eased 2bp to 3.92% (z +1.71, still flagged; 45th percentile since 1954 but the 67th of the last 30 years, †). Why this matters: a credit spread that widens on a day stocks rise is credit pricing in more default/liquidity risk even as equity sentiment improves — lenders aren't buying the relief rally yet, and historically that disagreement is worth more weight than the equity move alone.

The dollar (DXY) joined the hawkish-repricing side of the ledger: it rose 0.74% to 102.30 (newly flagged, z +1.64; 72nd/81st percentile, no real gap — cite either). Fed balance-sheet and TGA readings are still last Thursday's H.4.1/DTS release, carried forward unchanged — thin history, no pre-2008 comparison exists for either series (§4F). ON RRP, the nearly drained overnight-cash shock absorber, ticked up to $0.18B (z −0.53, not flagged). Why this matters: a strengthening dollar on a hot jobs print is the same signal as the front-end yield rise — markets pricing a Fed that holds higher for longer, which tightens financial conditions globally even without the Fed lifting a finger today.
history_html:
The 30-year Treasury's 5.26% first reached this level Jul 31 and has held on 47 of 69 sessions since, but before this run the last time was Jul 2007 — and only briefly, 15 sessions between May 2006 and Jul 2007 — with the level last routine before Feb 2002; every 1980s reading sat at or above today's level. Today sits at the 80th percentile of the last 30 years but only the 46th since 1977 — unusual lately, unremarkable on the fuller record, a gap worth citing both ways. Compared with Jul 2007: the 10-year then was 5.19% vs. 4.86% now (similar, both elevated by modern standards), the overnight policy rate then (fed funds, 5.22%) was well above today's SOFR (3.92% — not similar, the Fed has far less room used up today), and the curve was barely positive then (2s10s +20bp) vs. today's +35bp (similar, both un-inverted).

What's different from 2007 is this week's own pattern, not the level: credit widened again Friday even as equities bounced, and the front end of the curve did the day's repricing on a jobs beat that pushed Fed rate-hike odds higher — a hawkish, not dovish, growth story. The S&P 500's 0.31% gain is an ordinary-sized move (not a tail reading either direction) and sits 5.65% below its Oct. 6 closing high; this year's worst drawdown so far was 9.1%, well inside the 10.5% median since 1950.

For a client asking whether the bounce means the worst is over: the bond market's elevated level still keeps 2007 company, but what matters this morning is that credit didn't join Friday's equity relief — by this brief's own hierarchy (Unit 8, below), that unconfirmed gap is worth more attention than the headline index moves.
movers_html:
How this section works: 502 of 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically (KVUE unavailable), plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 61 name candidates and 1 sector divergence qualified Friday, well below Thursday's 167 — the cap holds at 3 names + 1 sector note. Earnings/guidance reactions prioritized per §5.

Axon Enterprise (AXON) −18.18% (313.00, from 382.56) — what happened: Friday's single largest decliner among qualifying names. Stated reason: Axon's Q3 2026 report (released Thursday) missed on both lines — non-GAAP EPS $1.72 vs. a $1.90 consensus, revenue $908.55M, about 2.4% light — and the company cut its 2026 growth outlook to roughly 30% from prior guidance while announcing a $1.2B Skydio drone-fleet acquisition funded partly by a new $1.15B convertible raise, lifting net debt to $1.2B (tikr.com, Barchart, citing the company's own release and EarningsWhispers data). Read-through: idiosyncratic — a company-specific guidance cut and a debt-funded acquisition, not a read on the broader AI-hardware complex; no macro read-through asserted.

Coherent (COHR) +13.58% (192.81, from 169.76) — what happened: one of the day's largest gainers, recovering more than its prior-session drop. Stated reason: Citi raised its price target to $440 from $420 Friday, the specific catalyst named in dated coverage (tikr.com); the move follows Thursday's roughly 14% drop on a Nov. 4 earnings report that had actually beaten the company's own guidance (revenue up 49.9% to $2.37B, adjusted EPS $2.09, Q2 revenue guided to $2.55–2.75B) — the market sold the beat Thursday and an analyst re-priced it Friday. Read-through: a demand-side AI-datacenter-optics data point (Unit 7's demand-vs-financing distinction) resolving positive two sessions after the print, not a same-day macro signal.

AMD +11.04% (449.04, from 404.40) — what happened: part of Friday's broad chip-sector bounce (Nvidia +2.8%, SanDisk +~4%, per Washington Post/Fox Business's Friday coverage). Stated reason: no dated, named-source reporting specific to AMD surfaced for Friday; broad coverage attributes the chip-sector bounce generically to a post-selloff recovery, with no single catalyst named. Read-through: the mirror image of Thursday's broad, catalyst-less selloff (CL-0063) — a bounce in the same names, on the same lack of individual news, is itself evidence the move is sentiment/positioning-driven rather than a reassessment of AI-capex fundamentals; CL-0063 (SMH, due 2026-11-13) remains the live test of whether it holds.

Sector note — Consumer Staples (XLP) −1.28% vs SPY +0.31%, a 1.59pp underperformance. Stated reason: no single-company catalyst found; the sector's laggard status fits a classic defensive-to-cyclical rotation on a recovery day. Read-through: a small, mechanical confirmation that Friday's bounce had some genuine risk-on character at the sector level, even though credit (Dashboard, above) didn't confirm it macro-wide.
chart_of_day_why: SMH remains this run's largest |z| move (−3.21, against +2.83 on HY OAS's Thursday print, the next-largest) even after Friday's 3.63% bounce — still the single most stretched reading on the board, and the chart most directly behind both today's movers story (AMD) and the live CL-0063 claim.

concept_title: When agreement doesn't last — reapplying the hierarchy the very next session
concept_html: Segment 2 showed the clean case: Thursday, stocks, credit, and bonds all moved together, and agreement across markets that don't have to agree was itself the strongest signal available. Friday hands the unit the next lesson, and it's an uncomfortable one: that agreement didn't survive one session. Stocks bounced; credit widened again; the dollar and the front end of the curve moved in the hawkish direction on a jobs report that argued for a less generous Fed, not a more generous one. Segment 1's hierarchy — when markets disagree, weight credit over equity sentiment — isn't a one-time tool you use once and retire. It has to be reapplied every single morning, because yesterday's agreement is not a standing fact about today's market; it's a reading that can and does expire. The discipline this teaches isn't “credit is always right” — it's that confirmation has to be checked fresh each day, the same way this brief reconciles its claims ledger fresh each morning rather than assuming yesterday's conclusion still holds.
client_translation: Just because the market agreed with itself yesterday doesn't mean it still does today -- check the signal fresh every morning instead of assuming it's still true.
client_lens_html:
“The market bounced back Friday, so are we past the worst of it?” Stocks did bounce, but the part of the market that tends to be the more reliable warning sign — credit spreads — got wider, not narrower, the same day. That disagreement, not the headline index number, is the thing worth watching into this week.

“I heard the jobs report was good — isn't that bullish?” A strong jobs report is good news about the economy, but it's being read by markets as raising the odds the Fed holds rates higher for longer (or even hikes in December), which is why short-term bond yields and the dollar rose Friday even as stocks rallied. Good economic news and a friendlier Fed don't always arrive together.

“What happened with Axon and Coherent?” Two unrelated, company-specific stories: Axon missed earnings and cut guidance (down 18%); Coherent, which had actually beaten its own earnings guidance Wednesday night but sold off anyway, got an analyst price-target upgrade Friday and partly recovered (up 14%). Neither is a read on the broader market — both are useful reminders that a single day's stock move can be about one company's numbers, not the macro picture.

  • New conditional claim CL-0064 (due 2026-11-16): tests which side of Friday's stock/credit divergence resolves correctly, per this week's Unit 8 teaching. Within 5 trading sessions: the S&P 500 closes below Thursday's $7,353.73 close while HY OAS and/or IG OAS stay flagged (|z| ≥ 1.5) → confirms credit's read (the bounce was the noise); HY OAS and IG OAS both ease below |z| 1.5 while the S&P 500 holds above Friday's $7,376.86 close → confirms equities' read (credit was lagging); any other combination expires as a mixed read. Figures from data/state.json.
  • New conditional claim CL-0065 (due 2026-11-10, tomorrow's CPI): tests whether Friday's front-end-led yield rise (2Y +5bp vs. 10Y +2bp, 2s10s flattening 3bp to 35bp) on the jobs beat was the start of a durable hawkish repricing. If tomorrow's Core CPI prints at or above 0.3% m/m (above the 0.2% consensus) and the 2-year yield closes at or above Friday's 4.51% → confirms a durable hawkish repricing; Core CPI prints at or below 0.1% and the 2-year yield closes back below 4.46% (Thursday's level) → refutes it as a one-day jobs-report reaction; anything else expires mixed. Figures from the BLS release and data/state.json.
